reason: The sources provide 18 verified, cross-referenced claims from multiple distinct sites detailing the New London School explosion of 1937, the money-saving tap into a raw gas line, the spark that ignited it, the devastation, and the legacy of gas odorization laws.
story: On March 18, 1937, the New London School in Texas—one of the wealthiest schools in America, built with oil boom riches—suddenly evaporated in a massive explosion. To save three hundred dollars a month, school trustees had bypassed commercial natural gas to tap into a local residue gas line. Because untreated natural gas is completely odorless, a slow leak under the school went unnoticed, completely filling the crawlspace. Just minutes before the final bell, manual training instructor Lemmie R. Butler flipped the switch on an electric sander. A tiny spark ignited the trapped gas, instantly launching the building’s roof and crushing hundreds of students and teachers. The tragedy claimed nearly three hundred lives. In the aftermath, a devastated public demanded action. The disaster directly inspired the Texas Engineering Practice Act and laws mandating that natural gas be mixed with a distinctively smelly chemical, mercaptan, ensuring gas leaks could never go unnoticed again.
angle: To save $300 a month, a wealthy Texas school tapped into a waste gas line; because the gas had no smell, a slow leak went undetected until a shop teacher flipped a sander's switch, causing an explosion that killed nearly 300 people and forced the invention of scented natural gas.

claims.claim: The New London School explosion occurred on March 18, 1937.

evidence.quote: The New London School explosion occurred on March 18, 1937
On March 18, 1937, a gas explosion occurred in a school in New London, Texas

claims.claim: The New London School district was considered one of the wealthiest in the country.

evidence.quote: the school district in New London, Texas (formerly known as London) was one of the richest in the United States.
The brand new, steel-and-concrete school, located in the East Texas Oilfield, was one of the wealthiest in the country.

claims.claim: The school board authorized tapping into Parade Gasoline Company's residue gas line to save money.

evidence.quote: the school board canceled their natural gas contract and had plumbers install a tap into Parade Gasoline Company's residue gas line to save money.
school officials had recently approved tapping into a residue gas line of the local Parade Gasoline Company, a common money-saving practice in the oilfield at the time.

claims.claim: The unrefined natural gas was odorless, which allowed the leak to go undetected.

evidence.quote: Untreated natural gas is both odorless and colorless, so leaks are difficult to detect and may go unnoticed.
Hundreds died at New London High School in Rusk County after odorless natural gas leaked into the basement and ignited.

claims.claim: Manual training teacher Lemmie R. Butler flipped the switch on an electric sander, triggering the explosion.

evidence.quote: At 3:17 p.m., Lemmie R. Butler, an "instructor of manual training," turned on an electric sander.

Manual arts teacher Lemmie R. Butler reached for the switch on a sanding machine, and, flipping it, unknowingly changed the lives of families in the small Rusk County town forever...and ended his own.

claims.claim: The sound of the massive explosion was heard up to four miles away.

evidence.quote: The explosion was its own alarm, reportedly heard up to four miles away from the school.
The sound of the explosion was heard four miles away.

claims.claim: The force of the blast threw a two-ton concrete block 200 feet, where it crushed a parked car.

evidence.quote: The force of the explosion was so great that a two-ton concrete block was thrown clear of the building and crushed a 1936 Chevrolet parked 200 feet away.
A two-ton concrete slab was flung 200 feet away by the force of the blast, smashing down upon a car.

claims.claim: Mother Frances Hospital in Tyler was scheduled to open the next day, but canceled its dedication and opened immediately to care for the wounded.

evidence.quote: A new hospital, Mother Frances Hospital in Tyler, was scheduled to open the next day, but the dedication was canceled and the hospital opened immediately.

The survivors were taken to Mother Frances Hospital in Tyler; the hospital’s administrators canceled an elaborate dedication ceremony which had been planned for that day, instead opening immediately in order to care for the wounded.

claims.claim: Walter Cronkite covered the disaster and later stated that no story since had equaled its magnitude.

evidence.quote: I did nothing in my studies nor in my life to prepare me for a story of the magnitude of that New London tragedy, nor has any story since that awful day equaled it.

Decades later, the retired CBS Evening News anchor added, “I did nothing in my studies nor in my life to prepare me for a story of the magnitude of that New London tragedy, nor has any story since that awful day equaled it.”

claims.claim: Texas passed a law requiring that malodorants be mixed into natural gas for commercial and industrial use.

evidence.quote: As a direct result of this incident, a Texas law mandated that malodorants be added to all natural gas for commercial and industrial use, a practice that is now an industry standard.
the State of Texas passed an odorization law, which required that malodorants be mixed in all gas for commercial and industrial use

claims.claim: Mercaptan is the chemical added to natural gas to give it a distinctive rotten-egg odor.

evidence.quote: Mercaptan, a harmless chemical, gives gas its distinctive rotten egg odor.
The now-mandated rotten-egg smell associated with natural gas is mercaptan, the odorant added to indicate the potentially dangerous leaking of gas.

claims.claim: Public pressure called for legislation to register engineers because poor engineering was believed to be partly to blame.

evidence.quote: Public pressure was on the government to regulate the practice of engineering due to the faulty installation of the natural gas connection
Public pressure called for legislation to register engineers, since it was believed that poor engineering had been at least partly to blame for the accident.

claims.claim: The school superintendent, who lost his own son in the blast, was forced to resign under pressure.

evidence.quote: Superintendent W. C. Shaw was forced to resign amid talk of a lynching. Shaw had lost a son, a niece and a nephew in the explosion.
The superintendent of schools, who himself had lost a son in the blast, was forced to resign under pressure from citizens in the school district.

claims.claim: For decades, community members were hesitant to speak about the explosion, often whispering about it.

evidence.quote: People were afraid to talk about it; almost no family in this community was unaffected, and whenever people would tell us about the explosion it would be sort of in whispers and don't say anything in front of so-and-so because they lost a sister.

People were afraid to talk about it; almost no family in this community was unaffected, and whenever people would tell us about the explosion, it would be sort of in whispers and don’t say anything in front of so-and-so because they lost a sister

claims.claim: A blackboard found in the ruins had a message noting that oil and natural gas were East Texas' greatest gifts or blessings.

evidence.quote: Reportedly, a blackboard at the destroyed school was found that read, "Oil and natural gas are East Texas’ greatest natural gifts. Without them, this school would not be here and none of us would be learning our lessons."
Sometime in the night a worker found a blackboard that had been on the wall that read ‘Oil and natural gas are East Texas’ greatest mineral blessing,'

claims.claim: The explosion killed nearly 300 students and teachers.

evidence.quote: On March 18, 1937, a gas explosion occurred in a school in New London, Texas, killing almost 300 of the 500 students and 40 teachers in the building.
In March 1937, a natural gas explosion killed nearly 300 of their classmates and teachers.

disputed: The exact death toll: S1 lists 425 killed and a later estimate of 294, S6 lists 298, S2 and S3 say nearly/almost 300, and S4 says about 300. The script should say 'nearly 300 children and teachers died' to remain general and uncontroversial.

The exact time of the explosion: S2 states the explosion occurred at 3:05 p.m., while S1, S6, and S7 place it at 3:17 p.m. The script should generalize this as 'just after 3 p.m.' or 'minutes before the final bell.'

The precise text on the recovered blackboard: S2 reports the board read 'Oil and natural gas are East Texas’ greatest natural gifts...' while S6 reports 'Oil and natural gas are East Texas’ greatest mineral blessing.' The script should attribute this as 'a blackboard found in the ruins praised oil and gas as the region's greatest blessing.'
